title: A dental pain pathway to reduce antibiotic prescribing in general practice: cluster randomised trial
subtitle: Eleven practices, allocation at practice level
statement: In three practices of an 11-practice network, 123 of 212 dental pain consultations over six months ended with an antibiotic prescription, often without planned dental treatment, in a district where many adults have no regular dentist. The network wants to test whether a dental pain pathway, with a short decision aid, a same-day dental telephone triage line and analgesia advice, reduces antibiotic prescribing for dental pain without increasing emergency attendances for dental infection, using a cluster randomised design.
whoAffected: Adults with toothache or facial swelling who consult general practices, especially those without a regular dentist; GPs and practice nurses; the community dental service; the microbiology team.
whatHurts: Antibiotics that do not relieve most dental pain, delayed dental treatment, adverse effects and antimicrobial resistance, and patients who return in pain.
currentPractice: GPs assess dental pain without dental access or a decision aid; antibiotics are commonly prescribed; there is no triage route to dental care.
whyNow: The community dental service can run a triage line for 12 months from January 2027, and the microbiology team is pressing for reduced prescribing.
constraints: The triage line exists only for 12 months from January 2027. Study work in practices is limited to routine data extraction by the network data team. No change to how practices code consultations.
patientCenteredGoal: People with toothache get pain relief and timely dental treatment, and antibiotics only when infection is spreading.
summary: Problem framed as a cluster randomised trial of a dental pain pathway in general practice.
